items.prompt: Which pattern ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global access point to it?

options.label: Decorator
Factory Method
Singleton
Observer

rubric: Singleton restricts a class to one instance with a global access point.
Factory Method is often confused with it because both concern object creation, but it does not limit the instance count.

items.prompt: Into which GoF category does the Observer pattern fall?

options.label: Behavioral
Architectural
Structural
Creational

rubric: Observer governs how objects communicate and distribute responsibility, so it is behavioral.
Structural is a common wrong pick because observers are linked to a subject.

items.prompt: What does the Strategy pattern define?

options.label: A single object shared across the whole program
A tree of objects treated uniformly as one
A wrapper that converts one interface into another
A family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface

rubric: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface.
The wrapper-converting option describes Adapter; the tree option describes Composite.

items.prompt: Which pattern attaches extra responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it?

options.label: Decorator
Singleton
Builder
Strategy

rubric: Decorator wraps an object to add behavior at runtime.
Strategy swaps behavior but does not wrap to add responsibilities.

items.prompt: In the Observer pattern, what is the object being watched, which notifies the others, usually called?

options.label: Subject
Builder
Context
Adapter

rubric: The watched object is the Subject (also called Publisher).
Context is the term used in Strategy, which is why it tempts learners.

items.prompt: Which of the following are creational patterns? Select all that apply.

options.label: Singleton
Decorator
Factory Method
Builder
Observer

rubric: Builder, Singleton and Factory Method all deal with object creation.
Observer is behavioral and Decorator is structural.

items.prompt: A team lead says: "Define an interface for creating an object, but let subclasses decide which concrete class to instantiate." A new developer wants to look up the name of this pattern in the GoF catalogue. Which name should they search for?

options.label: Prototype
Facade
Factory Method
Template Method

rubric: That wording is the GoF intent of Factory Method.
Template Method also uses subclasses but defines algorithm steps, not object creation.

items.prompt: A checkout class uses a long if/else chain to pick a discount algorithm. Why does replacing it with the Strategy pattern help?

options.label: It guarantees only one discount object is ever created
Each algorithm sits in its own class, so you can add or swap one without editing the checkout
It lets every discount be notified automatically when prices change
It hides the checkout class behind a simpler interface for clients

rubric: Strategy isolates each algorithm so the client is closed to modification when adding new ones.
Notification describes Observer and the simplified interface describes Facade.

items.prompt: A `TimedReader` class implements `Reader`, holds another `Reader`, forwards every call to it, and logs the elapsed time. Which pattern is this?

options.label: Decorator
Factory Method
Strategy
Singleton

rubric: It wraps an object with the same interface to add behavior, which is Decorator.
Strategy is tempting, but it swaps an algorithm rather than wrapping to extend.

items.prompt: Three widgets are registered as observers of a `Temperature` subject. The subject's value changes. What happens?

options.label: No widget is told until each one asks the subject for its value
Every registered widget is notified so it can update itself
The subject creates a new widget to display the new value
Only the first registered widget is told, because it registered first

rubric: Observer notifies all registered observers on a state change.
Polling is the opposite of Observer's push-style notification.

items.prompt: Why do many developers call a factory instead of using `new ConcreteClass()` directly in client code?

options.label: The factory lets the client skip implementing the interface
The factory ensures that the object can never be subclassed
The client depends on an abstraction and not on a specific concrete class
The factory makes object creation run faster than `new` does

rubric: Factories decouple the client from concrete classes, so the created type can change.
Speed is not the purpose of factories.

items.prompt: Why is the Singleton pattern often criticised in larger codebases?

options.label: It acts as hidden global state, which makes code harder to test and reason about
It stops a class from having any methods besides its constructor
It requires an inheritance hierarchy with many subclasses
It forces every class to implement an interface

rubric: Singleton behaves like global state, causing hidden coupling and testing difficulties.
The other options describe requirements that Singleton does not have.

items.prompt: Which statements about the Decorator pattern are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: It needs one subclass for every possible combination of features
A decorator implements the same interface as the object it wraps
It adds behavior without modifying the wrapped object's class
It replaces the wrapped object's class at compile time
Decorators can be stacked to combine behaviors at runtime

rubric: Decorators share the interface, stack, and extend behavior without altering the original class.
Avoiding a subclass per combination is the pattern's purpose, so that claim is reversed.

items.prompt: A weather dashboard has a chart, a text label and an alert banner. Each currently calls the data class repeatedly to check for new readings. The team wants the data class to push updates to whichever displays are open, without knowing their concrete types. Which pattern fits best?

options.label: Observer
Builder
Singleton
Decorator

rubric: Observer lets a subject notify any registered displays without knowing their types.
Decorator and Builder do not handle change notification.

items.prompt: What recurring problem does the Observer pattern address?

options.label: Objects need extra behavior added by wrapping them in another object with the same interface
Objects need to be created without the creating code naming the concrete class it instantiates
Objects need to swap one interchangeable algorithm for another while the program is running
Objects need to learn about a subject's changes without the subject knowing their concrete classes

rubric: Observer decouples a subject from the objects that react to its changes.
The distractors describe Factory, Strategy and Decorator.

items.prompt: Factory Method belongs to which category of GoF patterns, and why?

options.label: Creational, because it deals with how objects get created
Architectural, because it splits an application into layers
Structural, because it composes objects into larger structures
Behavioral, because it spreads responsibility between objects

rubric: Factory Method is creational because it abstracts object creation.
Structural and behavioral are other GoF categories; 'architectural' is not a GoF category.

items.prompt: A checkout method uses a long if/else chain on payment type. Why might replacing it with the Strategy pattern help?

options.label: Each payment algorithm sits in its own class behind one interface, so adding one needs no edit to the selecting code
Only one instance of each payment algorithm can exist, so state is never duplicated
Payment classes inherit shared fields from a common concrete base, so there is less repeated data
Method calls are cheaper than conditionals, so the checkout code runs noticeably faster

rubric: Strategy encapsulates each algorithm behind a shared interface so new ones can be added without modifying callers.
Distractors confuse Strategy with performance tuning, Singleton or inheritance reuse.

items.prompt: Why would a developer choose Decorator over creating a subclass for every feature combination?

options.label: It hides a complex subsystem behind one simple entry-point class for clients
It lets behaviors be combined at runtime by wrapping, so no subclass per combination is needed
It lets a class change its own superclass while the program is running
It ensures a wrapped object can never be reached directly by other code

rubric: Decorators stack at runtime and avoid a class explosion.
Distractors describe Facade or invented guarantees.

items.prompt: What is a common criticism of the Singleton pattern?

options.label: It forces every class to inherit from one abstract base class in the application
It forbids the instance from holding any data between separate method calls
It acts like global state, which hides dependencies and makes tests harder to isolate
It makes object creation slower for every other class in the application

rubric: Singletons behave like global state, coupling code and hurting testability.
Distractors are invented restrictions that Singleton does not impose.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe benefits of the Factory Method pattern? Select all that apply.

options.label: Products automatically notify each other when their state changes
Client code depends on a product interface rather than a concrete class
Only one product object can ever be created by the factory
New product types can be added with little change to client code

rubric: Factory Method decouples clients from concrete products and eases adding new ones.
Single-instance guarantees belong to Singleton and state notification to Observer.

items.prompt: A sensor class calls `update()` directly on `PhoneWidget`, `WebWidget` and `WatchWidget` whenever a reading changes. Every new widget type means editing the sensor class. Which explanation of the fix is correct?

options.label: Widgets subclass the sensor so they inherit the readings and need no notification
Widgets register through a common listener interface, so the sensor notifies them without knowing their classes
Each widget wraps the sensor in a decorator that forwards the readings to the widget
A factory creates the right widget per reading, so the sensor never needs to call any widget

rubric: Observer lets widgets subscribe through an interface so the sensor stays unchanged for new widgets.
Distractors misapply inheritance, Decorator and Factory.

items.prompt: A `Cart` holds a `Discount` field and its `total(s)` returns `discount.apply(s)`. Which change adds a 'half price' rule in the Strategy style?

options.label: Make `Cart` extend a new `HalfPrice` class so it overrides `total`
Add a `boolean half` flag to `Cart` and an if statement inside `total`
Turn `Discount` into a singleton that stores the half price rule inside it
Add a `HalfPrice` class implementing `Discount` and pass it to the `Cart`

rubric: Strategy adds a new class implementing the shared interface and injects it.
Distractors reintroduce conditionals, misuse inheritance or misuse Singleton.

items.prompt: `Espresso.cost()` returns 2.0. `Sugar` and `Milk` are decorators adding 0.5 and 0.7 to the cost of the object they wrap. What does `new Milk(new Sugar(new Espresso())).cost()` return?
rubric: Each decorator adds its own cost to the wrapped cost: 2.0 + 0.5 + 0.7 = 3.2.
Other values drop one or more layers of wrapping.

items.prompt: A subject has observers A and B registered. Then B unregisters, and `setState()` is called; it ends by notifying all registered observers. Which observers receive the update?

options.label: Both A and B
Only A
Only B
Neither A nor B

rubric: Only observers still registered are notified, so A alone.
Distractors assume unregistration is ignored or that nothing gets notified.

items.prompt: A report exporter must be a `PdfExporter` or `CsvExporter` depending on a setting, and calling code should only use the `Exporter` interface. Which pattern fits best?

options.label: Factory method
Decorator
Singleton
Observer

rubric: Factory Method hides which concrete class is created behind an interface.
The other patterns address notification, wrapping and single instances.

items.prompt: Which implementation correctly gives a Singleton in a class `Config`?

options.label: A private constructor plus a static method that returns one stored `Config` instance
A final class with only static fields and a public constructor for callers
A private constructor plus a public static method that returns a new `Config` each call
A public constructor plus a static counter that logs duplicate objects

rubric: A private constructor with a static accessor returning one stored instance enforces a single object.
Distractors still allow multiple instances to be created.

items.prompt: Which tasks are good fits for the Observer pattern? Select all that apply.

options.label: Notifying every subscriber when a new article is published
Adding a gift wrapping cost to an order by wrapping the order object
Updating a chart and a table whenever a data model changes
Choosing between bubble sort and quick sort based on input size

rubric: Both fit one-to-many change notification.
Choosing algorithms is Strategy and wrapping to add cost is Decorator.

items.prompt: A file app has a `DataStream` interface with `read()`. The team wants encryption and compression layers, usable in any combination or order, without writing a class for every combination. Which design applies the right pattern?

options.label: Write subclasses for each combination, such as `EncryptedCompressedStream` and `CompressedEncryptedStream`
Add boolean flags to `DataStream` and branch on them inside every `read()` call
Create a singleton `StreamManager` that always applies the layers in one fixed order
Write `EncryptedStream` and `CompressedStream` classes that implement `DataStream` and wrap another `DataStream`

rubric: Decorators implement the same interface and wrap another instance, so layers combine freely.
Distractors cause class explosion, flag-driven branching or a rigid order.

items.prompt: A checkout page lets customers pick flat-rate, weight-based or express shipping at runtime. Each option has its own cost formula, and more carriers will be added later. Which design applies a fitting pattern?

options.label: An observer list where every carrier is notified when checkout starts
A `ShippingStrategy` interface with one class per formula, injected into checkout
A `Shipping` singleton holding one global cost formula that checkout reads
A decorator chain where each carrier wraps the previous carrier's cost

rubric: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms selected at runtime, so new carriers need no checkout changes.
Distractors confuse Strategy with Singleton, Decorator or Observer.

items.prompt: A subject calls `update(v)` on its observers in attach order. Code: `attach(Logger); attach(Display); attach(Alarm); detach(Display); set(7)`. Logger prints `L7`, Display prints `D7`, Alarm prints `A7`. What is printed?
rubric: Display was detached before `set`, so only Logger and Alarm are notified, in attach order.
`L7 D7 A7` ignores the detach; `A7 L7` ignores ordering.

items.prompt: `Coffee.cost()` returns 2.0. Decorators add to the wrapped cost: `Milk` adds 0.5 and `Sugar` adds 0.2. What does `Sugar(Milk(Milk(Coffee()))).cost()` return?
rubric: Each decorator adds its amount to the wrapped result: 2.0 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.2 = 3.2.
2.7 counts Milk once; 2.2 counts only Sugar.

items.prompt: A `Dialog` base class calls an overridable `createButton()` inside `render()`. `WinDialog` overrides it to return `WinButton`. You must add macOS support using Factory Method with minimal change to existing code. What do you do?

options.label: Add `MacDialog` that overrides `createButton()` to return `MacButton`
Make `MacButton` a decorator that wraps `WinButton` inside `WinDialog`
Add an `if os == mac` branch inside `Dialog.render()` that builds `MacButton`
Make `WinDialog` a singleton and subclass it to produce macOS buttons

rubric: Factory Method lets a subclass decide which product to create, leaving `render()` untouched.
The `if` branch modifies existing code and defeats the pattern.

items.prompt: A Singleton's `getInstance()` does `if (inst == null) inst = new Config()`. Two threads can call it at once and both see null. Which change guarantees a single instance?

options.label: Mark the `inst` field private so threads cannot read it simultaneously
Add a second null check right after the first, without any locking
Create the instance in a static initializer so it exists before any call
Make the `Config` constructor public so each thread can verify it

rubric: Eager creation by the class loader removes the race entirely.
A repeated check without synchronisation or visibility guarantees still races; access modifiers do not control threading.

items.prompt: Which situations are fitting uses of the Strategy pattern? Select all that apply.

options.label: Adding optional borders and scrollbars to a window at runtime
Swapping between ZIP and GZIP compression based on a user setting
Letting a sorter use comparison rules supplied by the caller
Ensuring only one logger object exists in the whole process
Notifying several screens when a stock price changes

rubric: Strategy swaps interchangeable algorithms such as compression or comparison rules.
The other options describe Singleton, Observer and Decorator.

items.prompt: A text editor must support multi-step undo for typing, deleting, pasting and formatting. Each action changes the document differently. You decide to apply the Command pattern. Which implementation step fits?

options.label: Wrap each action in an object with `execute()` and `undo()`, and push executed ones on a stack
Decorate the editor with `UndoEditor`, which deletes the last typed character on undo
Make the editor an observer of itself so each change triggers a reverse change automatically
Create a factory that builds a new editor per keystroke and discards the older ones

rubric: Command objects encapsulate an action and its reversal, and a stack gives multi-step undo.
The decorator option only handles typing, not pasting or formatting.

items.prompt: `Document.publish()`, `edit()` and `approve()` each start with a long `if status == 'draft' ... elif 'review' ... elif 'published'` chain. Adding an 'archived' status means editing all three methods. What is the root cause and fitting remedy?

options.label: Creation logic is scattered across methods; add an abstract factory that builds a document per status
Callers are never told about status changes; add an observer so each method can react to them
Behaviour is fixed at construction time; wrap the document in a decorator for each status
Status-dependent behaviour is scattered across methods; extract one State class per status and delegate

rubric: The same state conditional is duplicated, which State centralises per status.
Other patterns address creation, notification or added responsibilities, not state-driven behaviour.

items.prompt: A long-lived `PriceFeed` notifies `ChartView` objects. Users open and close many charts; memory keeps growing and closed charts still log updates. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The feed uses Observer instead of Strategy, so views are never freed
Closed views never called `detach`, so the feed's list still references them
Each view creates its own feed, so feeds multiply with every chart opened
The `notify` loop iterates in order, which keeps early views alive longer

rubric: This is the lapsed-listener problem: the subject holds strong references to observers never removed.
Other options misattribute the leak to the pattern choice or iteration order.

items.prompt: A `Stream` class has subclasses `EncryptedStream`, `BufferedStream`, `EncryptedBufferedStream`, `CompressedEncryptedStream` and so on; the class count doubles with each new feature. What does this reveal, and why does Decorator help?

options.label: Subclasses override too many methods, so decorators remove the need for any shared stream interface
Streams should exist once per process, so decorators guarantee one stream instance per feature
Inheritance is slower at runtime, so decorators avoid virtual dispatch when features are combined
Features vary independently, but inheritance fixes combinations at compile time; decorators compose them at runtime

rubric: Independent optional features cause combinatorial subclassing; decorators wrap one another to compose behaviour.
Decorators still require a shared interface, and the performance or instance-count claims are wrong.

items.prompt: Tests pass individually but fail in random order. Each test calls `Settings.getInstance().set('mode', 'x')` with different values. Which analysis best explains the failures?

options.label: Singletons forbid reading values, so each test sees stale copies of the settings
Singletons are created lazily, so whichever test runs first is slow and times out
The `Settings` class is final, so tests cannot subclass it to reset its values
State held by the single global instance leaks between tests, so results depend on run order

rubric: A Singleton is hidden shared global state that persists across tests, creating order dependence.
The other options invent laziness, finality or read restrictions as causes.

items.prompt: `Sorter` holds a `CompareRule` object that the client sets. `Connection` holds a `ConnState` object and replaces it itself after each call. Both delegate to an interface. Which comparison is accurate?

options.label: Both are Decorator because each one wraps another object to extend its behaviour
Both are Strategy because both delegate work to an object behind an interface
`Sorter` is Strategy since the client picks the algorithm; `Connection` is State since transitions happen internally
`Sorter` is State because behaviour changes; `Connection` is Strategy because it holds a reference

rubric: Structure is similar; the difference is intent: client-chosen algorithm versus self-driven state transitions.
Delegation alone does not identify a pattern.

items.prompt: A team uses Observer among 12 components. Which symptoms point to problems caused by this design? Select all that apply.

options.label: One update triggers cascades of notifications that are hard to trace
Adding a new subclass requires editing existing `if` chains
An observer that throws can stop later observers from being notified
The result depends on the order in which observers were attached
The subject must be modified to support each new observer type

rubric: Cascades, order dependence and exception propagation are known Observer pitfalls.
Editing `if` chains and modifying the subject are not Observer drawbacks; Observer avoids the latter.

items.prompt: A `Repo` is wrapped by two decorators: `AuthCheck` (throws if the user lacks rights) and `Cache` (returns stored results by id). It is deployed as `Cache(AuthCheck(Repo))`. A user without rights can read records that another user loaded earlier. Why?

options.label: Decorators share one state, so `Cache` overwrote the second user's rights; use one decorator
The outer cache answers hits before the call reaches `AuthCheck`; wrap as `AuthCheck(Cache(Repo))`
`AuthCheck` runs first and clears the cache on each call, exposing records; reverse the order
`Repo` is a singleton so rights persist between users; remove both decorators entirely

rubric: Decorator order matters: the outermost decorator sees the call first, so cache hits skip authorisation.
Other options invent shared state or cache clearing that decorators do not cause.

items.prompt: A long-running UI app registers a `PriceListener` on a global `PriceFeed` each time a panel opens. After panels are closed, they stay in memory and keep reacting to updates. What is the root cause?

options.label: Listeners implement an interface instead of extending a base class, so the runtime cannot track their lifetimes properly.
The feed keeps strong references to listeners that were never unregistered, so closed panels remain reachable.
The feed notifies listeners synchronously, and that prevents the garbage collector from reclaiming them once the callback returns.
The feed is global, and a global object duplicates every listener it receives, leaving extra copies in memory.

rubric: Observer subjects hold references to subscribers, so a missed unsubscribe keeps them alive (the lapsed listener problem).
Distractors blame synchronous dispatch or global scope, which do not by themselves retain objects.

items.prompt: A team builds `new EncryptingStream(new CompressingStream(fileStream))` and writes text through it. The files come out nearly as large as the uncompressed text. Why?

options.label: The compressing decorator is wrapped by another decorator, and wrapped decorators fall back to a pass-through mode.
Writes reach the outer decorator first, so data is encrypted before compression, and ciphertext is nearly incompressible.
Decorators must be stacked with the cheapest operation outermost, otherwise the inner one silently disables itself.
Each decorator copies the data into its own buffer, so the compressor only sees a small fragment of every write.

rubric: Decorator order determines the order of processing; compressing after encrypting is ineffective because ciphertext looks random.
Distractors invent decorator rules that do not exist.

items.prompt: A `Document` holds a `Policy` object behind an interface. The document itself replaces its policy as it moves Draft, Review, Published, and each policy decides which policy comes next. Which analysis fits best?

options.label: It is Strategy, because the behavior sits in an interchangeable object that is held behind a common interface.
It is State, because the context's own transitions swap the behavior object, whereas Strategy leaves that choice to the client.
It is Observer, because each policy is notified whenever the document changes status and reacts to it.
It is Decorator, because each policy wraps the previous one and layers extra behavior on top of it.

rubric: The distinguishing feature is who changes the object and why: self-driven transitions indicate State.
Strategy is the strongest distractor because the structure is nearly identical.

items.prompt: Tests pass when run alone but some fail in the full suite, in varying order. The code calls `Config.getInstance()` everywhere, and one test sets a flag on it. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The singleton is not thread-safe at creation, so two instances are created and tests randomly receive different ones.
Singletons cannot hold flags, so the flag write is silently ignored and later tests read stale default settings.
The singleton's mutable state survives between tests, so outcomes depend on run order, and call sites hide that dependency.
The test runner reloads classes between tests, which resets the singleton and drops values that other tests rely on.

rubric: Shared global state leaks across tests, causing order-dependent failures.
Thread-safety is a real singleton issue but does not explain order-dependent failures in a sequential suite.

items.prompt: A toolkit creates widgets via `ButtonFactory.create(theme)` and `CheckboxFactory.create(theme)`. After a mid-render theme switch, dark buttons appear beside light checkboxes. Which structural weakness explains this?

options.label: The factories should be singletons, so each theme has only one button instance and one checkbox instance in the app.
Nothing ties the products to one family: theme is passed per call, so one factory per family would keep them consistent.
The widgets lack a shared base interface, so the theme cannot be applied uniformly across the products it creates.
Factory method is overused here, and replacing the factories with direct constructors would guarantee matching themes.

rubric: Abstract Factory enforces that related products come from the same family; per-call theme arguments can drift.
Distractors treat the symptom as a singleton or interface problem.

items.prompt: A subject notifies observers by looping over its live observer list. Which problems can this cause? Select all that apply.

options.label: An observer that unsubscribes itself inside its callback can trigger a concurrent-modification error or make the next observer be skipped.
Notifying a copy of the list guarantees an observer unsubscribed mid-loop will never receive the in-flight event.
An observer that subscribes a new observer mid-notification can make delivery of the current event inconsistent.
Iterating the live list makes the subject unable to notify observers in the order they registered.

rubric: Mutating the list during iteration causes skipped or inconsistent delivery.
Iterating a copy still delivers to observers removed mid-loop, and live iteration does not alter ordering.

items.prompt: A service builds reads as `LoggingRepo(CachingRepo(SqlRepo))`. A nightly batch job writes through a separate `SqlRepo` instance created directly. Afterwards users see stale records until the cache expires. What explains this?

options.label: Decorators must subclass the concrete `SqlRepo`, so the cache cannot observe changes made by a sibling instance.
`LoggingRepo` sits outside `CachingRepo`, so it intercepts reads first and prevents them from ever reaching the cache layer.
The batch writes bypass the decorator chain, so the cache never sees the updates and cannot invalidate entries.
`CachingRepo` should be a Proxy rather than a Decorator, because decorators cannot keep state between successive calls.

rubric: A decorator only intercepts calls routed through it; a second write path avoids the cache invalidation.
Distractors misstate decorator rules about ordering, inheritance and state.

items.prompt: A shipping method has two cost rules, standard and express, fixed by contract for years and used in one six-line method. Criteria: minimal code, readability, no expected new variants. Which approach is best?

options.label: Use Abstract Factory to build rule objects, so the rules can be swapped through a configuration file later on.
Introduce a Strategy interface now, because adding it later always forces a rewrite of every caller in the codebase.
Keep a simple conditional in that method, since two stable variants don't justify extra types or indirection.
Use Template Method with one subclass per rule, because inheritance avoids passing strategy objects around the code.

rubric: With two stable variants, a patterns-based design adds cost without benefit; this is the overengineering trap.
Distractors justify patterns with speculative future needs.

items.prompt: A service needs exactly one connection pool per process. Criteria: unit tests must substitute a fake pool, and dependencies must be visible in signatures. Which design best meets these?

options.label: Create the pool once at startup and inject it into consumers, keeping one instance without a global accessor.
A classic Singleton with `getInstance()`, since it guarantees one instance and tests can reset it using reflection.
A new pool created inside each consumer, since separate pools keep tests independent and the cost is negligible.
A static utility class, since its stateless static methods can be replaced in tests by writing a subclass.

rubric: Single instance by construction plus injection satisfies both criteria.
A classic Singleton hides dependencies, and per-consumer pools violate the one-pool requirement.

items.prompt: An order service publishes `OrderPlaced` to six subscribers. The email subscriber sometimes takes 5 seconds or fails. Criteria: checkout latency under 50 ms, subscriber failures must not affect checkout, eventual delivery is acceptable. Which is best?

options.label: Use a Singleton event manager, since a single shared instance guarantees that events are delivered in under 50 ms.
Replace Observer with direct calls to six services in sequence, so each failure is handled right where it occurs.
Dispatch events through a queue or executor, so slow or failing subscribers cannot block the publisher.
Keep synchronous Observer and wrap each callback in try/catch, which also removes the delay caused by slow subscribers.

rubric: Decoupling delivery from publishing via asynchronous dispatch meets the latency and isolation criteria.
try/catch handles failures but not slowness, and the other options do not remove blocking.

items.prompt: A data sink offers optional compression, encryption, buffering and logging, chosen per deployment at runtime in any combination and order. Criteria: no class explosion, features testable independently, configurable order. Which design is best?

options.label: Decorators sharing the sink interface, composed at startup in the configured order.
A subclass for every combination of features, because inheritance keeps each variant's behavior explicit and testable.
One sink class with four boolean flags, because a single class is simplest and the flags choose features per deployment.
A Template Method base with a hook per feature, overridden by one subclass for each deployment configuration.

rubric: Decorators compose independent features in any order without a combinatorial class count.
Subclasses explode, flags fix the order, and Template Method needs a subclass per configuration.

items.prompt: An AST has 30 node types, and a new node type is added nearly every release, while only two operations (print, evaluate) exist. A teammate proposes Visitor. Criterion: minimise edits per new node type. How do you judge it?

options.label: Weak fit: every new node type forces edits to all visitors, so methods on the nodes localise change better.
Weak fit: Visitor cannot traverse tree structures, so a Composite with recursive calls is required instead of it.
Strong fit: Visitor removes the need for node classes to share an interface, which reduces edits per new node type.
Strong fit: Visitor lets new node types be added without touching existing visitors, since dispatch happens dynamically.

rubric: Visitor makes adding operations easy but adding element types costly; here types change often and operations are stable.
Distractors reverse that trade-off or claim Visitor cannot traverse trees.

items.prompt: A team is choosing between Strategy and Template Method for varying an algorithm. Which situations favour Strategy? Select all that apply.

options.label: The same algorithm should be reused by several unrelated classes without inheritance.
Subclasses must override fixed steps while the base class controls the overall sequence.
The variants need direct access to the host class's protected members, with no interface.
The algorithm must be swapped at runtime on an object that already exists.

rubric: Strategy uses composition, so it supports runtime swapping and reuse across unrelated classes.
Fixed sequencing and protected access are traits of Template Method's inheritance.

items.prompt: A `ReportConfig` has 3 required and 8 optional fields, must be immutable, and cross-field rules (end date after start date) must hold for every instance. Criteria: readable call sites and no invalid instances. Which design is best?

options.label: A Builder with named setters, whose `build()` validates cross-field rules and returns an immutable object.
A constructor overloaded for each combination of optional fields, repeating the validation in each constructor.
A Prototype cloned from a default object, with callers changing fields on the clone as they need.
A mutable object with setters and a separate `validate()` method that callers invoke before they use it.

rubric: Builder gives readable construction and a single validation point that prevents invalid instances.
Overloads are unreadable at this scale; mutable setters and cloning allow invalid or changing states.

items.prompt: A large service needs exactly one shared `Config` object at runtime. Criteria: unit tests must substitute alternate configs in parallel, and the lifetime must still be single-instance. Which approach best satisfies them?

options.label: Create one instance at startup and inject it through constructors
A static utility class that reads the config file on every call
A global mutable variable that tests overwrite and then restore
A classic Singleton with a static `getInstance()` called from every class

rubric: Constructor injection keeps a single instance while letting tests pass substitutes, so the single-instance requirement is not coupled to global access.
Static Singleton and globals hide dependencies and make parallel tests interfere with each other.

items.prompt: A stream class must support any combination of compression, encryption and checksumming, chosen at runtime per connection. Criteria: avoid a class explosion and allow stacking in any order. Which design is the best fit?

options.label: Wrap the stream in decorators that each add one behaviour
One stream class with boolean flags and a long `if` chain
A subclass for every combination, such as `EncryptedCompressedStream`
A Template Method base class with overridable hook steps

rubric: Decorators compose independent behaviours at runtime in any order without a combinatorial number of classes.
Subclassing per combination explodes in size and is fixed at compile time; flags and hooks fix the order and bloat one class.

items.prompt: A long-lived event bus uses Observer with strong references. Short-lived UI panels subscribe on creation and are discarded without any cleanup call. Which is the most serious flaw in this design?

options.label: Notifications are synchronous, so each subscriber runs in order
The bus keeps discarded panels reachable, so they leak memory and still receive events
Subscribers cannot know which other subscribers exist
The bus depends on an abstract observer interface, not concrete panel classes

rubric: The lapsed listener problem: a long-lived subject holding strong references keeps dead observers alive and calling them.
The other options describe normal or intended properties of Observer, not defects.

items.prompt: In a language with first-class functions, a team wants to vary one pricing calculation by customer type. The criteria are minimal code and no future need for strategy state or multiple methods. Which choice is best?

options.label: Define a `PricingStrategy` interface with one class per customer type
Pass the pricing function as a parameter to the caller
Subclass `Customer` and override a `price()` method in each subclass
Use an Abstract Factory that builds pricing strategy families

rubric: With first-class functions and a single behaviour, a function argument is the Strategy pattern without ceremony.
The other options add classes or hierarchies the stated criteria rule out.

items.prompt: A UI toolkit must ship Windows-style and Mac-style widget sets. Criterion: an application must never mix a button from one style with a checkbox from the other. Which creational pattern best enforces this?

options.label: Builder that assembles each widget step by step
Factory Method on each widget class, chosen independently per widget
Abstract Factory with one concrete factory per style
Prototype cloning of individual widgets from a shared registry

rubric: Abstract Factory creates whole families of related products from one factory, so consistency is structural.
Independent per-widget creation lets styles mix, which is the misconception the distractors share.

items.prompt: A team applies Visitor to an AST whose node types keep being added, while new operations are rare. Which criticisms of this choice are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Visitors usually need node internals exposed, weakening encapsulation
Each new node type forces a change to every existing visitor
Double dispatch cannot be done in single-dispatch languages at all
Adding a new operation requires editing every node class

rubric: Visitor makes adding operations easy but adding element types costly, and it often exposes node state.
Adding operations without touching nodes is the benefit, and double dispatch is emulated via accept/visit.

items.prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS team uses a Singleton `ConnectionPool` for its database. Product now wants a dedicated pool per large tenant, with limits set per tenant, plus integration tests with a fake pool. Which judgment of the Singleton and the best revision is most sound?

options.label: Replace it with a pool provider keyed by tenant, injected where needed
Make the Singleton thread-safe with double-checked locking and keep it
Turn the pool into static methods so no instance is needed at all
Keep the Singleton and add a `tenantId` parameter to every query call

rubric: Per-tenant pools and fakes need multiple, substitutable instances, so an injected provider or registry keyed by tenant fits.
Thread-safe Singleton or statics still force exactly one global pool and block substitution.

items.prompt: Design an editor's undo feature. Constraints: each user action is undoable, a recorded sequence of actions can be undone as one step, and actions can be nested. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: Memento snapshots of the whole document taken after every keystroke
Observer listeners that log each change and replay them in reverse
A Strategy per action type chosen by a large switch on the action name
Command objects with `undo()` and a composite macro command grouping them

rubric: Command gives per-action undo and Composite macro commands give grouped, nestable undo.
Whole-document snapshots and reverse event logs do not provide structured grouping and nesting.

items.prompt: An order moves through states such as draft, paid, shipped and cancelled. The allowed operations differ per state and new states are expected. Constraint: no growing `if`/`switch` over a status field in every method. Which design fits?

options.label: A Singleton `OrderManager` that checks the status before every call
State objects that implement the operations, with the order delegating to the current one
A Decorator chain that wraps the order once for each state it has passed
An `Order` with a status enum and a switch inside each method

rubric: The State pattern moves state-specific behaviour into separate classes and the order delegates, so adding a state adds a class.
Enum switches and manager checks keep the conditionals; decorators model added behaviour, not exclusive states.

items.prompt: Design the integration with two payment vendors whose SDKs have different method names. Constraints: domain code must not import vendor types, vendors must be swappable, and domain tests must run without network access. Which design meets all three?

options.label: A domain-owned `PaymentGateway` interface, one adapter per vendor, and a fake for tests
Call each SDK directly and wrap each call in a try/catch for errors
One Singleton class that exposes both SDKs and picks one by a flag
A Facade that returns the vendor SDK response objects to the domain unchanged

rubric: A domain-owned port with vendor adapters isolates vendor types and allows a test fake.
Passing vendor objects through or using a flag leaks vendor details into the domain.

items.prompt: A `Report` has 12 optional settings, must be immutable once created, and must reject invalid combinations such as a chart without a data source. Which design meets all constraints?

options.label: A Prototype that clones a default `Report` and lets callers edit the clone
A Builder that collects settings and validates them in `build()`, returning an immutable `Report`
A mutable `Report` with setters and a `validate()` method callers should invoke
A constructor with 12 parameters where callers pass null for the unused ones

rubric: Builder accumulates optional settings, validates the combination once in build(), and yields an immutable object.
Setters and prototype edits leave the object mutable; long constructors do not check combinations.

items.prompt: A framework defines a fixed import workflow: read, validate, transform, save. Constraints: plugin authors customise individual steps but must never reorder or skip steps. Which design meets this?

options.label: An Observer where plugins subscribe to events for each step name
A Template Method with a final `run()` calling overridable step methods
A Factory that returns the plugin's own workflow class on request
A Strategy interface with one `run()` method that plugins implement fully

rubric: A final template method fixes the skeleton while subclasses override only the steps.
A whole-workflow strategy, event subscription or plugin-owned workflow lets plugins control ordering.

items.prompt: A proposed Observer design for a multi-threaded service has subjects with `subscribe`, `unsubscribe` and `notify`, iterating directly over a shared list. Observers may unsubscribe during notification and may throw. Which additions would the design need? Select all that apply.

options.label: Require observers to extend a concrete base class to be registered
Iterate over a snapshot of the observer list when notifying
Catch and isolate each observer's exception so the others still run
Make `notify` private so that only the subject class can call it

rubric: A snapshot avoids concurrent modification when observers unsubscribe, and isolating exceptions stops one failing observer from blocking the rest.
Making notify private or requiring a concrete base class addresses neither requirement.

items.prompt: A reporting tool exports to PDF and CSV. Third parties must be able to add formats such as XLSX by dropping in a library, without recompiling the tool, and users pick the format by name at runtime. Which design meets these constraints?

options.label: A Singleton `Exporter` with a `format` flag that holds all of the export code
An `Exporter` interface and a name-keyed registry where plugins register their implementations
A subclass of `Report` per format, with the tool compiled against all of them
A `switch` on the format name that is edited whenever a new format is added

rubric: A common interface plus a registry (factory) keyed by name lets plugins add formats without changing the core.
Switches, compiled-in subclasses and a flagged Singleton all require changing or recompiling core code.
